doc_name: List of presidents of the Philippines
text: Under the Constitution of the Philippines, the president is both the head of state and government and serves as the commander-in-chief of the armed forces. The president is directly elected by qualified voters to a six-year term and must be a natural-born citizen of the Philippines, a registered voter, able to read and write, at least forty years of age on the day of the election, and a resident of the Philippines for at least ten years immediately preceding the election. No elected president can seek re-election; however, a successor who has not served more than four years can still run for a full term. Upon resignation or removal, the vice president assumes the presidency. The incumbent president is Bongbong Marcos, who assumed office on June 30, 2022. Emilio Aguinaldo became the first president of the Philippines under the Malolos Republic, known as the First Philippine Republic, which he led until 1901 when he was captured by U.S. forces during the Philippine–American War (1899–1902). The American colonization of the Philippines abolished the First Republic, leading to the U.S. governor-general exercising executive power. In 1935, the United States, fulfilling its promise of full Philippine sovereignty, established the Commonwealth of the Philippines following the ratification of the 1935 Constitution, which restored the presidency. The first national presidential election was held, and Manuel L. Quezon (1935–1944) was elected to a six-year term with no re-election provision as the second Philippine president and first Commonwealth president. In 1940, the Constitution was amended to allow re-election but shortened the term to four years. Three years later, the Second Philippine Republic was established under the 1943 Constitution imposed by Japan after the occupation of the Philippines in 1942 during World War II. José P. Laurel served as puppet president of the Japanese-sponsored government; his de facto presidency, not legally recognized until the 1960s, overlapped with the Commonwealth president, who went into exile. The Second Republic ended after Japan's surrender in 1945, and the Commonwealth was restored that year with Sergio Osmeña (1944–1946) elected as president. Manuel Roxas (1946–1948) succeeded Osmeña after winning the first post-war election in 1946 and became the first president of the independent Philippines when the Commonwealth ended on July 4 of that year, marking the beginning of the Third Republic, which included the administrations of the next five presidents, the last being Ferdinand Marcos (1965–1986), who imposed martial law in 1972 and established the New Society (Bagong Lipunan), leading to the Fourth Republic. Marcos's dictatorship ended in 1986 with his deposition during the People Power Revolution, and the current constitution came into effect in 1987, beginning the Fifth Republic. Among those elected as president, three died in office: Manuel L. Quezon and Manuel Roxas by natural causes, and Ramon Magsaysay in a plane crash (1953–1957). Ferdinand Marcos is the longest-serving president, with 20 years and 57 days in office, making him the only president to serve more than two terms; Sergio Osmeña is the shortest-serving, having served 1 year and 300 days. Two women have held the presidency: Corazon Aquino (1986–1992), who became president following the successful People Power Revolution of 1986, and Gloria Macapagal Arroyo (2001–2010), who ascended to the presidency as vice president upon Estrada's resignation and was later elected to a full six-year term in 2004. Some historians consider Andrés Bonifacio the first president of the Philippines; he was the third Supreme President of the Katipunan, which he transformed into a revolutionary government known as the Tagalog Republic upon the Cry of Balintawak in August 1896. While the term "Tagalog" referred to a specific ethnicity, Bonifacio used it to represent all indigenous Filipinos, replacing the colonial term "Filipino." Some historians argue that including Bonifacio as a president should also include Macario Sakay and Miguel Malvar, who continued Aguinaldo's leadership after his capture and revived the Tagalog Republic in 1902, respectively. These individuals are considered "unofficial presidents" by some scholars and are not recognized as presidents by the Philippine government. Emilio Aguinaldo is officially recognized as the first president of the Philippines, based on his term during the Malolos Republic, though he had previously led several revolutionary governments that are not counted in the official succession of Philippine republics. Manuel L. Quezon delegated his presidential duties to José Abad Santos, then-Chief Justice, when he fled the Philippines during Japanese occupation to establish a government-in-exile; Abad Santos is believed to have functioned as acting president, though no legal document confirms the transfer of the presidency. Three former vice presidents—S. Laurel, Binay, and Robredo—have made unsuccessful runs for the presidency. The list provided includes only cabinet secretaries who served full-time; vice presidents who served concurrently as cabinet secretaries are not included.
